front: Pearly papule with telangiectasia and a rolled border on the nose versus a scaly, ulcerated lesion on a sun-damaged ear: which cancers, and who needs Mohs?
bottom: BCC and SCC: biopsy, then excise.

bullets.clue: BCC: pearly, rolled border. SCC: scaly, crusted; can metastasize.
bullets.treat: Low-risk: excise (BCC 4 mm, SCC 4–6 mm margins). High-risk: Mohs.
bullets.trap: Ear, lip, recurrent or perineural lesions are high risk.

back: BCC and SCC: biopsy, then excise. Key clue: BCC: pearly, rolled border. SCC: scaly, crusted; can metastasize. First-line: Low-risk: excise (BCC 4 mm, SCC 4–6 mm margins). High-risk: Mohs. Exam trap: Ear, lip, recurrent or perineural lesions are high risk.

diagram.alt: Basal cell carcinoma is pearly with a rolled border; squamous cell carcinoma is scaly and ulcerated; excise low-risk lesions and use Mohs surgery for high-risk sites.

source.guideline: AAD Guidelines of care for the management of basal cell carcinoma; and for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: AAD 2018: surgical excision with 4 mm clinical margins for low-risk BCC; Mohs for high-risk BCC; for low-risk cutaneous SCC, standard excision with 4–6 mm margins; Mohs for high-risk SCC.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Itchy, relapsing rash on an infant's cheeks and extensors, and in an adult's flexures: diagnosis and treatment ladder?
bottom: Atopic dermatitis: moisturize plus topical anti-inflammatories.

bullets.clue: Chronic itch, flexural in older patients, personal or family atopy.
bullets.treat: Emollients plus topical steroid or calcineurin inhibitor; dupilumab if severe.
bullets.trap: Routine antibiotics don't help; vesicles with fever: eczema herpeticum.

back: Atopic dermatitis: moisturize plus topical anti-inflammatories. Key clue: Chronic itch, flexural in older patients, personal or family atopy. First-line: Emollients plus topical steroid or calcineurin inhibitor; dupilumab if severe. Exam trap: Routine antibiotics don't help; vesicles with fever: eczema herpeticum.

diagram.alt: Atopic dermatitis: itchy relapsing rash on cheeks in infants and flexures in adults; treat with emollients and topical steroids; dupilumab for severe disease.

source.guideline: AAD Guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis in adults with topical therapies; with phototherapy and systemic therapies
source.recommendation: AAD 2023 topical therapies: emollients/moisturizers; topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors; routine use of topical antimicrobials not recommended. AAD 2024: systemic options including dupilumab for moderate-to-severe disease.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Silvery plaques on the elbows and knees, nail pitting, pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted: diagnosis, treatment, and what to screen for?
bottom: Plaque psoriasis: topicals if mild, biologics if moderate–severe.

bullets.clue: Silver scale, Auspitz sign, nail pitting, Koebner phenomenon.
bullets.treat: Topical steroid plus vitamin D analog; biologic for moderate–severe.
bullets.trap: Screen for psoriatic arthritis; systemic steroids can rebound.

back: Plaque psoriasis: topicals if mild, biologics if moderate–severe. Key clue: Silver scale, Auspitz sign, nail pitting, Koebner phenomenon. First-line: Topical steroid plus vitamin D analog; biologic for moderate–severe. Exam trap: Screen for psoriatic arthritis; systemic steroids can rebound.
mnemonic: Auspitz bleeding, pitting nails, Koebner at scars

diagram.alt: Plaque psoriasis: silvery scale on extensor surfaces, Auspitz sign, nail pitting and Koebner phenomenon; treat mild disease topically and moderate to severe disease with biologics.

source.guideline: Joint AAD-NPF guidelines of care for the management and treatment of psoriasis with biologics
source.recommendation: AAD-NPF 2019: biologics (TNF, IL-12/23, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors) are monotherapy options for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis; comorbidity guideline (alt link) recommends screening for psoriatic arthritis.

front: Why do comedones form, and what is first-line topical therapy for inflammatory acne?
bottom: Follicular plugging plus Cutibacterium acnes inflammation.

bullets.treat: AAD 2024: topical retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide.
bullets.trap: Do not combine a tetracycline with isotretinoin.

back: Follicular plugging plus Cutibacterium acnes inflammation. Key clue: Comedones define acne. First-line: AAD 2024: topical retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide. Exam trap: Do not combine a tetracycline with isotretinoin.

diagram.alt: Follicular plugging plus Cutibacterium acnes inflammation.

source.guideline: AAD Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris
source.recommendation: AAD 2024: topical benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, antibiotics (combine with BPO), oral doxycycline for moderate–severe inflammatory acne, isotretinoin for severe or scarring/refractory acne; avoid antibiotic monotherapy.

front: Painful rash with mucosal erosions and skin sloughing two weeks after a new drug, versus a rash with eosinophilia and hepatitis three weeks in: diagnoses and first step?
bottom: SJS/TEN versus DRESS: stop the culprit drug now.

bullets.clue: SJS/TEN: Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosions. DRESS: eosinophilia, organ injury.
bullets.treat: TEN: burn unit or ICU supportive care. DRESS: steroids if organs involved.
bullets.trap: Culprits: allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides; never rechallenge.

back: SJS/TEN versus DRESS: stop the culprit drug now. Key clue: SJS/TEN: Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosions. DRESS: eosinophilia, organ injury. First-line: TEN: burn unit or ICU supportive care. DRESS: steroids if organs involved. Exam trap: Culprits: allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides; never rechallenge.

diagram.alt: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis cause mucosal erosions and skin sloughing; DRESS causes rash with eosinophilia and organ injury; stop the culprit drug.

source.guideline: Society of Dermatology Hospitalists supportive care guidelines for the management of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis in adults
source.recommendation: SDH 2020 supportive care guideline for SJS/TEN in adults (title/abstract level only); stopping the culprit drug and ICU/burn-unit supportive care are standard first steps.

task_area: Health Maintenance, Patient Education, and Preventive Measures
front: Who should be counseled to reduce skin-cancer risk, and what is the advice?
bottom: Fair-skinned young people, from 6 months through 24 years.

bullets.clue: USPSTF 2018 grade B, still the posted recommendation.
bullets.trap: A changing pigmented lesion is biopsied. Counseling does not replace that.

back: Fair-skinned young people, from 6 months through 24 years. Key clue: USPSTF 2018 grade B, still the posted recommendation. First-line: Shade, clothing, and broad-spectrum sunscreen. Exam trap: A changing pigmented lesion is biopsied. Counseling does not replace that.

diagram.alt: Fair-skinned young people, from 6 months through 24 years.

source.guideline: USPSTF Skin Cancer Prevention: Behavioral Counseling (2018, still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: AFP 2025: confirm tinea with KOH; topical antifungals for corporis/cruris/pedis; oral terbinafine first-line for tinea capitis. CDC: permethrin 5% cream from the neck down for 8–14 h, repeat in about one week if needed.

front: Adult with partial-thickness burns over 30% of body surface: how is fluid resuscitation started, and which burns go to a burn center?
bottom: Start lactated Ringer's by %TBSA; titrate to urine output.

bullets.clue: Rule of nines; partial-thickness: blisters, painful. Full-thickness: leathery, painless.
bullets.treat: ABA 2023: start 2 mL/kg per %TBSA over 24 h.
bullets.trap: Classic Parkland uses 4 mL/kg; over-resuscitation harms.

back: Start lactated Ringer's by %TBSA; titrate to urine output. Key clue: Rule of nines; partial-thickness: blisters, painful. Full-thickness: leathery, painless. First-line: ABA 2023: start 2 mL/kg per %TBSA over 24 h. Exam trap: Classic Parkland uses 4 mL/kg; over-resuscitation harms.

diagram.alt: Burn resuscitation: start lactated Ringer's at 2 milliliters per kilogram per percent body surface area over 24 hours and titrate to urine output; refer major burns to a burn center.

source.guideline: American Burn Association Clinical Practice Guidelines on Burn Shock Resuscitation; ABA Guidelines for Burn Patient Referral
source.recommendation: ABA 2023 burn shock CPG: adults with ≥20% TBSA burns: initiate resuscitation at about 2 mL/kg/%TBSA, titrated to urine output; ABA referral guidelines: full-thickness, partial-thickness ≥10% TBSA, face/hands/feet/genitalia/joints, inhalation, chemical and high-voltage injuries.

task_area: History Taking and Performing Physical Examination
front: Sacral wound in a bedbound patient: how do stages 1 to 4, unstageable and deep tissue injury differ on exam?
bottom: Depth sets stage: dermis 2, fat 3, muscle or bone 4.

bullets.clue: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema.
bullets.trap: Slough or eschar hiding the base: unstageable. Maroon, non-blanchable: deep tissue.

back: Depth sets stage: dermis 2, fat 3, muscle or bone 4. Key clue: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. First-line: Offload pressure: reposition; support surface. Exam trap: Slough or eschar hiding the base: unstageable. Maroon, non-blanchable: deep tissue.

diagram.alt: Pressure injury stages: stage 1 intact skin with non-blanchable erythema, stage 2 partial thickness with dermis, stage 3 full thickness with fat, stage 4 exposed muscle or bone; unstageable when slough or eschar hides the base; deep tissue injury is maroon non-blanchable skin.

source.guideline: NPIAP Pressure Injury Stages (2016 staging system); International Guideline: Prevention and Treatment of Pressure Ulcers/Injuries, 4th edition (EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA, 2026) (still current as of 2026)
source.recommendation: NPIAP 2016 staging: stage 1 intact skin with localized non-blanchable erythema; stage 2 partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis; stage 3 full-thickness skin loss with visible fat; stage 4 full-thickness loss with exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone; unstageable when slough or eschar obscures the wound base; deep tissue pressure injury is persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration. International Guideline 2026 has chapters on classification, repositioning and mobilization, support surfaces and heel pressure injuries.
